blocks.text: Consider an RLC series circuit connected to an AC source of variable frequency (Fig 17.11 a). In its impedance diagram (Fig 17.11 b), the inductive reactance XL = wL and the capacitive reactance XC = 1/(wC) point in opposite directions. So the impedance is Z = square root of (R^2 + (XL - XC)^2) (17.24) = square root of (R^2 + (wL - 1/(wC))^2) (17.25).

blocks.alt: (a) R, L and C in series with an AC source, current I. Beside them three small graphs against time: for R, Vo and Io in step; for L, Io with Vo a quarter cycle ahead; for C, Io with Vo a quarter cycle behind. A rotating phasor circle shows XL at +90 degrees, XC at -90 degrees, 180 degrees apart. (b) Impedance triangle ABC: R along AB, XL - XC up BC, and Z along AC at angle theta.
blocks.caption: Figure 17.11 (a), (b): (a) RLC-series circuit with its AC source phasor diagram; (b) the impedance vector diagram of RLC-series circuit (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 17.11 (a), (b)).

blocks.text: At high frequency XL = wL is much greater than XC = 1/(wC), so the inductance dominates and the circuit behaves like an RL series circuit. At low frequency XC dominates and it behaves like an RC series circuit. In between there is a frequency wr at which XL = XC: the reactances, equal and opposite, cancel, and the circuit behaves as a purely resistive circuit (Fig 17.11 c). This condition is called resonance. From wr L = 1/(wr C): wr^2 = 1/(LC), wr = 1/square root of (LC), and since wr = 2 pi fr, the resonant frequency is fr = 1/(2 pi square root of (LC)) (17.26).

blocks.alt: (c) A single horizontal arrow R: at XL = XC only the resistance remains. (d) Current I against frequency f: a sharp peak at the resonance frequency fr, with a dashed line at the peak, a double arrow from the axis to the peak and horizontal arrows on both sides of the curve.
blocks.caption: Figure 17.11 (c), (d): (c) Vector diagram showing that the RLC-series circuit behaves as a pure resistive R-circuit at XL = XC; (d) RLC-series circuit resonance at XL = XC (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 17.11 (c), (d)).

blocks.text: Key properties of an RLC series circuit

items: Impedance and resonance: at resonance the impedance is a minimum, Z = R, and fr = 1/(2 pi square root of (LC)).
Current: at resonance the current is at its maximum because the impedance is a minimum (Fig 17.11 d).
Phase angle: at resonance it is zero; voltage and current are in phase and the power factor is 1.

Damping: the resistor damps the oscillations of the current; higher resistance gives more damping. A car's suspension is a mechanical analogue: the shock absorber dissipates energy like the resistance, and the mass and spring set the resonant frequency (Fig 17.11 e).

Tuning and filtering: RLC series circuits at resonance are used to tune radio receivers and in other communication devices, and as band-pass filters that let a chosen range of frequencies through while weakening others.
Voltage amplification: at resonance the voltages across the inductor and the capacitor can each be much larger than the applied voltage.
Power: the true power is P = VI cos(theta) (17.27), greatest when theta = 0, that is, at resonance or for a pure resistance.

blocks.text: In an LCR circuit the voltages across the inductor, capacitor and resistor are VL = 20 V, VC = 11 V and VR = 12 V. Find the phase difference between the resultant voltage and the current, and the rms voltage of the source. Solution: tan(theta) = (VL - VC)/VR = (20 V - 11 V)/12 V = 0.75, so theta = tan^-1(0.75) = 36.9 degrees. Vrms = square root of [VR^2 + (VL - VC)^2] = square root of [(12 V)^2 + (9 V)^2] = square root of 225 V^2 = 15 V.
